subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Turning Bodies: Full, Half, and Quarter Turns

tasks_in_class.description: Keep turning around; freeze when teacher says 'Statue'. Notice how much you have turned from your original position.
Identify the child who made a full turn and the child who made a half turn. Give examples of real-life situations involving turns.

time_bands.activity: The class plays Let us play Statue, p.32 ("keep turning; freeze when teacher says Statue") — children take turns spinning and freezing while the teacher prompts: 'How far did you turn from where you started?' Groups compare positions and informally name full, half, and quarter turns using body orientation as evidence.

Whole-class discussion using Discuss, p.32 ("identify the child who made a full turn…") — children pick out classmates who landed facing forward (full turn), backward (half turn), or sideways (quarter turn); they share real-life examples of objects that make each kind of turn, building a class list on the board.

Pairs revisit the 'Statue' positions: one partner slowly turns while the other calls 'stop' at a full, half, or quarter turn; the turner names the turn made. The class draws simple arrow sketches in notebooks to record the three turn types alongside a real-life example each.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often conflate the amount turned with the direction they face after turning; prompt them to compare their final facing with their starting facing, not with a fixed room direction. The idea that a half turn leaves you facing exactly backward is the key insight to draw out during discussion. Flag the common error: children saying they 'turned a full turn' whenever they spin at all — invite them to check by asking whether they face the same direction as at the start.
materials: Chalkboard or whiteboard for class list

periods.activity_title: Combining Turns and Exploring Everyday Objects

tasks_in_class.description: Complete: 2 half turns = ___ turn; 2 quarter turns = ___ turn; 4 quarter turns = ___ turn.
For each object (clothes clip, door with hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover) tick the maximum possible turn: less than 1/4, exactly 1/4, or more than 1/4.
Hold green straw steady; turn yellow straw. Observe different turns of the yellow straw using Pragya's straw-and-paper-clip model.

time_bands.activity: Introduce Fill in, p.33 ("complete: 2 half turns = ___ turn…") — the class acts out each combination physically before writing: two children each make a half-turn consecutively and verify they have together made a full turn; the same for quarter turns. Children record the three completed sentences.

Small groups work on Check and tick table, p.33 ("tick the maximum possible turn for each object…") — each group handles a real or imagined object (clothes clip, door, tongs, scissors, file cover), physically opens or rotates it as far as it will go, judges whether that is less than, exactly, or more than a quarter turn, and ticks accordingly. Groups share and resolve disagreements.

Pairs build Pragya's model as described in Observe, p.33 ("hold green straw steady; turn yellow straw…") using two straws and a paper clip; one partner holds the base straw while the other rotates the second straw to positions called out — full, half, quarter — and the pair identifies the turn made. Children sketch two positions in notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently confuse the maximum turn an object makes with the turn they personally apply to open it; redirect by asking 'How far can it go before it stops?' rather than 'How far did you move it?' Additional practice items Write, p.33 and Check and tick bullets, p.33 can be used as independent classwork or set for consolidation. A common error is marking scissors as a quarter turn because the blades cross — demonstrate that scissors open well past a quarter turn.
materials: Real objects or pictures: clothes clip, scissors, file cover

periods.activity_title: Paper Fan: Linking Turns to Angle Names

tasks_in_class.description: Make a paper fan by folding rectangular paper every 2 cm and pasting ice cream sticks. Use the fan to show different acute and obtuse angles.
Look at angles A–H marked on the notebook-cover house. Write whether each is right, acute, or obtuse.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Do acute-turns question, p.35
tasks_in_class.description: Make an acute turn with straws or fan, then make another acute turn. Determine whether the two acute turns together can form another acute turn.

homework.description: Make a 5-sided shape with 2 right angles, 2 obtuse angles, and 1 acute angle in your notebook.

time_bands.activity: Children make the paper fan as described in Let Us Do Q(a), p.34 ("fold rectangular paper every 2 cm; paste ice cream sticks…") — the teacher demonstrates one fold cycle, then children work independently. Once fans are ready, the teacher calls out angle types — 'show me an acute angle', 'show me a right angle' — and children open their fans to match; partners check each other.

Individually, children complete Let Us Do Q(b), p.35 ("look at angles A–H on the notebook-cover house…") — they use their fan as a reference tool, opening it to a right-angle position and comparing each labelled angle to decide right, acute, or obtuse. A few children share answers and justify: 'Angle C is acute because the fan opening is smaller than a right angle.'

Pairs investigate Let Us Do acute-turns question, p.35 ("make an acute turn, then another acute turn…") using straws or fans — they try combinations of small acute openings and observe whether the result stays acute, becomes right, or turns obtuse. Pairs record their finding in one sentence and share with the class, building toward the generalisation that two acute angles can add up to more than a right angle.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have explored turns as body rotations and object movements now connect that kinetic experience to named angle types; drawing attention to the fan's positions alongside the straw model helps reinforce that the amount of opening is the turn. A frequent error is calling all 'pointy' angles acute and all 'wide' angles obtuse — use the fan's right-angle position as the precise benchmark. The homework shape-drawing task (Let Us Do Q(c), p.35) asks children to apply all three angle types in one figure.
materials: Rectangular strips of paper (one per child)

tasks_in_class.description: Cut a circle from tracing paper, fold into 8 equal parts, attach straw at centre, mark starting point.

Show 1/8, 2/8, 1/4, 3/8 turns of the straw. Identify angle type for 2/8 and 4/8 turns. Continue to 5/8, 6/8, 7/8, 8/8; check when 3/4 and full turn are complete. Cut 1/8 and 2/8 parts and paste on card as measuring tools.

time_bands.activity: Children follow Angle Measuring Tool Q(a), p.36 ("cut a circle from tracing paper; fold into 8 equal parts; attach straw at centre; mark starting point") — the teacher models the first two folds on a large demonstration circle, then children complete the folding independently. The class counts the fold lines together to confirm eight equal sectors before attaching straws.

Children work through Angle Measuring Tool Q(b), p.36 ("show 1/8, 2/8, 1/4, 3/8 turns; identify angle type for 2/8 and 4/8; continue to 8/8…") — partners take turns rotating the straw to each fraction while the other names the angle type; they complete the sequence to a full turn and identify the 3/4-turn position. Children then cut the 1/8 and 2/8 sectors and paste them on card.

Quick class discussion: 'Which turn gives a right angle? Which gives a straight angle?' — children hold up their tools and show the 2/8 and 4/8 positions. The teacher records the angle-type table on the board (matching the fan summary from the earlier angle-types unit) so children can compare the two representations.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have connected turn amount to angle names using the paper fan are now building a precise measuring device; pointing out that each fold produces one-eighth of a full turn ties the fraction to the physical action. A common error is unequal folds that misalign sectors — emphasise folding the circle exactly in half first, then in half again, and again. The card-mounted 1/8 and 2/8 sectors will be used as measuring tools in the tasks that follow in this section.
materials: Tracing paper circles (one per child, pre-cut or scissors)

section_titles: Angle Measuring Tool — Sixths and Twelfths
periods.activity_title: Measuring Angles and Building Sixths Tools

tasks_in_class.description: Guess the measure of each angle shown; then check using the angle-measuring tool (use combinations). State whether each is acute, right, or obtuse.

Cut a circle from tracing paper; fold in half then into 3 equal parts. Attach straw, mark starting point; show turns of 1/6, 2/6, … full circle. Cut 1/6 and 2/6 parts; fold 1/6 in half to make 1/12. Paste on card as measuring tools.
In circles showing endpoints of 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 turns, draw arrows to show the starting points.

time_bands.activity: Children use their card-mounted eighths tools to work through Let Us Do Q1, p.38 ("guess the measure of each angle shown; then check using the angle-measuring tool…") — they first write a guess in fraction-of-a-turn form, then lay the 1/8 or 2/8 sector against the drawn angle and adjust their estimate; they record the verified measure and name the angle type.

Children make the sixths measuring tool as described in Angle Measuring Tool sixths, p.37 ("fold a tracing-paper circle in half then into 3 equal parts; attach straw; mark starting point; show 1/6, 2/6… turns; cut 1/6 and 2/6 sectors; fold 1/6 in half for 1/12; paste on card") — the teacher models the fold into thirds before children work in pairs.

Children tackle Let Us Think Q1, p.37 ("in circles showing endpoints of 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 turns, draw arrows to show starting points") — they reason backwards: 'If the arrow ends here after a 1/4 turn, where must it have begun?' Partners discuss before drawing; the class compares answers and justifies.

periods.teacher_notes: The estimate-then-verify sequence in the angle-measurement task builds the habit of checking intuition against a tool; praise children who revise their guess rather than those who guess correctly on the first try. Folding a circle into thirds is harder than folding into halves — allow time and demonstrate that each of the three layers must be equal when the circle is held up to light. Children who confuse clockwise and anti-clockwise starting positions in the backwards-arrow task can be prompted to physically rotate their own pencil the named fraction to feel the direction.
materials: Card-mounted 1/8 and 2/8 sectors from previous unit

periods.activity_title: Using the Tools: Arrow Turns and Shape Angles

tasks_in_class.description: Guess the measure of turns made by the arrow in cases (a)–(d). Verify using combinations of angle-measuring tools.
Measure each angle in the given shapes (a), (b), (c). Write measures in terms of turns; describe each as acute, obtuse, or right.
Draw angles for given measures of turns (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/12, 1/4) using the given lines.

time_bands.activity: Children complete Let Us Do Q2, p.38 ("guess the measure of turns made by the arrow in cases (a)–(d); verify using combinations of tools") — pairs write a guess for each arrow diagram, then overlay their sector tools to verify; they record the fraction of a full turn and compare guesses with verified values.

Children measure the angles inside shapes in Let Us Do Q3, p.38 ("measure each angle in shapes (a), (b), (c); write in terms of turns; name each as acute, obtuse, or right") — they place the sector tool at each vertex of the shape, read off the fraction, and record; partners cross-check by swapping notebooks.

Children draw angles for Let Us Do Q4, p.39 ("draw angles for given turn measures using the given lines") — they use their sector tools as guides, aligning the tool's edge with the given line and drawing the second ray at the correct fraction. Children label each drawn angle with its fraction and type.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have used the folded-circle tools to identify and name angles by fraction are now applying those tools to both reading and drawing — a fuller round-trip between picture and measure. A common error in shape measurement is placing the tool's centre off the vertex; demonstrate that the centre point must sit exactly at the corner. Where children struggle to draw the second ray freehand, suggest lightly tracing the tool's edge.

periods.activity_title: Drawing Turns and Clock Hand Problems

tasks_in_class.description: Draw the angles formed by: 1/2, 1/4, 2/4, 1/6, 4/6, 3/12, 1/2+1/4, and 1/8+1/6 turns in your notebook.

Find the turn made by the minute hand for each time interval [(a) 15 min, (b) 30 min, (c) 45 min, (d) 1/12 full turn → ? min, (e) full turn → ? min, (f) 1/6 full turn → ? min, (g) 4/12 full turn → ? min]; draw final clock positions.

time_bands.activity: Children work through Let Us Do Q5, p.39 ("draw the angles formed by 1/2, 1/4, 2/4, 1/6, 4/6, 3/12, 1/2+1/4, and 1/8+1/6 turns") — they use sector tools to set the angle, draw both rays from a common point, and label each with its fraction. The combined-fraction cases (1/2+1/4, 1/8+1/6) prompt children to physically stack the tools end-to-end before drawing.

Children solve Let Us Do Q6(a)–(g), p.39 ("find the turn made by the minute hand for each time interval; draw final clock positions") — they first reason that one full turn takes 60 minutes, then write the fraction for each interval and draw the final clock hand position. The teacher circulates and invites a child to explain the link between 15 minutes and 1/4 turn aloud.

A quick show-and-check: teacher calls out one of the clock problems (e.g., 45 minutes) and children hold up their notebooks showing the drawn clock hand; the class verifies together that 45 minutes gives a 3/4 turn.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have practised drawing individual turn-fractions now combine fractions and connect the fraction idea to a familiar moving object — the clock's minute hand. The key reasoning step is that a full turn of 60 minutes means each minute is 1/60 of a turn; children who struggle can be prompted to think in quarter-turns first ('how many quarter-turns fit into 60 minutes?'). A common error is drawing the clock hand from the edge of the clock face rather than from its centre.

periods.activity_title: Clockwise and Anti-clockwise: Direction of Turns

tasks_in_class.description: For each of the four creature pairs making a quarter turn, tick whether the movement is clockwise or anti-clockwise.
Observe direction while opening a tap, unscrewing a lid, and loosening a nut. Determine whether each moves clockwise or anti-clockwise.

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces clockwise and anti-clockwise direction by drawing a clock face on the board and tracing the hands' movement; children then mimic each direction with a finger in the air and confirm agreement. The class discusses: 'What is the same about clockwise and anti-clockwise? What is different?'

Children complete Tick direction, p.40 ("for each of the four creature pairs making a quarter turn, tick whether the movement is clockwise or anti-clockwise") — they examine each creature's before-and-after position, use their finger to trace the shortest arc of the quarter turn, and decide the direction. Small groups compare and resolve any disagreements.

Children carry out Try these, p.40 ("observe direction while opening a tap, unscrewing a lid, and loosening a nut…") — using a tap in the classroom or a jar lid brought in, children turn each object and identify the direction. They record their findings in a two-column table (object | clockwise or anti-clockwise) and share results, noting which everyday objects turn in each direction.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have explored the amount of turns across the chapter now add the dimension of direction; connecting the new vocabulary to the clock they see daily makes the terms concrete. A frequent error is confusing the direction of the arc with the direction the object ends up pointing — emphasise tracing the path of the movement, not the position of the result. If a classroom tap is not accessible, a bottle cap or a pencil sharpener works equally well for the hands-on observation.
materials: Clock face drawn on board or a demonstration clock
A tap, jar lid, or bottle cap for hands-on observation

periods.activity_title: Compass Turns: Applying Angles to Directions

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the table: given starting direction and turns (e.g., 'North, two right angles clockwise'), fill in the ending direction for all 7 rows.
Padma faces the toy shop. Determine what place she faces after a half turn clockwise. Find another way she can turn to face the same place.

time_bands.activity: The teacher labels the four classroom walls North, South, East, West with paper signs; children stand, face North, and make a clockwise right-angle turn — they check which wall they face (East) and discuss why. The class builds the four-direction compass on the board, noting that a right-angle clockwise turn moves N→E→S→W and anti-clockwise goes N→W→S→E.

Children complete Fun with Turns Q1, p.41 ("complete the table: given starting direction and turns, fill in ending direction for all 7 rows") — they work individually, optionally standing and physically making each turn to verify before writing. After completing the table, pairs compare answers and reconcile any differences.

The class discusses Fun with Turns Q2, p.41 ("Padma faces the toy shop; what does she face after a half turn clockwise; find another way to reach the same facing") — children first solve the half-turn problem, then in pairs brainstorm an alternative sequence of turns (e.g., two quarter turns anti-clockwise) that produces the same result. Each pair shares one alternative, and the class verifies together.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have built angle vocabulary, measuring tools, and direction labels across the chapter apply them together in a spatial reasoning context; the compass-direction puzzle is the most integrative task of the chapter and rewards children who have a secure sense of clockwise versus anti-clockwise. A common error is treating the four compass directions as fixed labels on the body rather than on the ground — if a child turns and thinks North moves with them, prompt them to re-read the wall labels. For Fun with Turns Q2, accept any combination of turns that produces the correct final direction and verify by acting it out.
materials: Paper signs labelling four classroom walls N/S/E/W

items.prompt: Renu stands facing the blackboard. She turns and now faces the back wall directly. What kind of turn did she make?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A half turn
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A half turn reverses your facing direction completely, so the front becomes the back.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks any large turn is a full turn, without connecting full turn to returning to the start.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses a quarter turn (which lands you sideways) with the halfway reversal.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not recognise that a change in facing direction implies a turn occurred.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child stand up and physically turn to feel the half turn; stretch: ask what turn brings her back to the blackboard.

exercise.description: Keep turning around; freeze when teacher says 'Statue'. Notice how much you have turned from your original position.

items.prompt: Look at a pair of scissors. Open them as wide as they will go. Do they make a turn that is less than a quarter turn, exactly a quarter turn, or more than a quarter turn? Write your answer and explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: More than a quarter turn. The blades of scissors open well past the position of a right angle, so the maximum turn is more than a quarter turn.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the fully opened angle of the scissors blades to a known quarter-turn position.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child physically open a real pair of scissors and compare to a folded quarter-circle; stretch: ask which object from the lesson makes exactly a quarter turn and how they know.

exercise.description: For each object (clothes clip, door with hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover) tick the maximum possible turn: less than 1/4, exactly 1/4, or more than 1/4.

items.prompt: A paper fan is opened to a position that is more than a quarter turn but less than a half turn. What type of angle does the fan show?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Obtuse angle
teacher_guide.method_one_line: An obtuse angle is the one produced by a turn between a quarter turn and a half turn.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses an acute angle (less than a quarter turn) with one greater than a quarter turn.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student thinks any turn near a quarter turn is a right angle, not distinguishing exactly a quarter from more than a quarter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student associates the word 'large' with straight angle, not recognising that a straight angle requires a full half turn.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child use a paper fan to physically land between the quarter and half positions and compare; stretch: ask the child to name what angle would come next if the fan opened even further.

exercise.description: Make a paper fan by folding rectangular paper every 2 cm and pasting ice cream sticks. Use the fan to show different acute and obtuse angles.

items.prompt: A tracing-paper circle is folded into 8 equal parts and a straw is attached at the centre. The straw is turned to show 3/8 of a full turn. Write the name of the angle type this turn produces and explain how you can tell using the folded circle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Obtuse angle. Three eighths of a turn is more than two eighths (which is a right angle) but less than four eighths (which is a straight angle), so the angle is obtuse.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare 3/8 to the right-angle benchmark of 2/8 and the straight-angle benchmark of 4/8 on the folded circle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to count the fold lines up to 2/8 and then 4/8 to bracket 3/8; stretch: ask what fraction of a full turn would produce an acute angle and give one example.

exercise.description: Cut a circle from tracing paper, fold into 8 equal parts, attach straw at centre, mark starting point.

items.section_title: Angle Measuring Tool — Sixths and Twelfths
items.prompt: A circle is folded into 6 equal parts. The straw is turned to show 2/6 of a full turn. Which angle type does this produce?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Acute angle. 2/6 of a full turn equals 1/3, which is less than 1/4 turn? No — 1/4 = 3/12 and 2/6 = 4/12, so 2/6 > 1/4. Revised: 2/6 equals 4/12 of a full turn; a right angle is 2/8 = 3/12 of a full turn; 4/12 > 3/12, so 2/6 is more than a right angle — this is an obtuse angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare 2/6 to the right-angle benchmark of 1/4 turn by converting to twelfths: 2/6 = 4/12, right angle = 3/12, so 2/6 is greater than a right angle.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student incorrectly identifies 2/6 as a right angle, confusing it with 2/8.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student associates any fraction with a denominator of 6 with a large angle.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child convert both fractions to twelfths to compare; stretch: ask the child to find a sixth-circle turn that gives an acute angle.

exercise.description: Cut a circle from tracing paper; fold in half then into 3 equal parts. Attach straw, mark starting point; show turns of 1/6, 2/6, … full circle. Cut 1/6 and 2/6 parts; fold 1/6 in half to make 1/12. Paste on card as measuring tools.

items.prompt: Meena opens a jar lid by turning it. The lid moves in the opposite direction to the way clock hands move. Which direction is the lid turning?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Anti-clockwise
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Clockwise matches the direction of clock hands; the opposite direction is anti-clockwise.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has the two direction labels swapped.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses the amount of a turn (full turn) with the direction of a turn.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student uses an angle-type term (straight) in place of a direction term, showing confusion between the two ideas.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child trace a clock face with a finger clockwise, then trace the opposite way and name it; stretch: name two more everyday objects that turn anti-clockwise when opened.

exercise.description: Observe direction while opening a tap, unscrewing a lid, and loosening a nut. Determine whether each moves clockwise or anti-clockwise.

items.prompt: Arjun starts facing East. He makes two quarter turns, both in the same direction. What direction does he face now? Explain your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: He faces West. Two quarter turns in the same direction equal a half turn, and a half turn reverses your facing direction, so East becomes West.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Two quarter turns combine to make a half turn, which reverses the starting direction.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to stand and physically make each quarter turn; stretch: ask what direction Arjun faces if he makes one more quarter turn in the same direction.

exercise.description: Identify the child who made a full turn and the child who made a half turn. Give examples of real-life situations involving turns.

items.prompt: Priya says: 'Four quarter turns make a full turn.' Is she correct? Write yes or no and explain why using numbers of turns.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes. Two quarter turns make a half turn, and two half turns make a full turn, so four quarter turns make a full turn.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Build up: 2 quarter turns = 1 half turn; 2 half turns = 1 full turn; so 4 quarter turns = 1 full turn.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child act out each quarter turn physically and count; stretch: ask how many eighth turns make a full turn and how they know.

exercise.description: Complete: 2 half turns = ___ turn; 2 quarter turns = ___ turn; 4 quarter turns = ___ turn.

items.prompt: A door with a hinge opens as wide as it possibly can. Which best describes the maximum turn the door makes?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: More than a quarter turn. A hinged door can swing open well past a right angle before it hits a wall or stop.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the fully open door's position to the right-angle benchmark of a quarter turn.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student underestimates the door's range of motion, perhaps thinking of a small gap.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student applies a quarter-turn label to any opening, confusing the benchmark with a maximum.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not recognise that a door cannot spin freely in a complete circle.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mime opening a door and compare the final position to a right angle drawn on paper; stretch: name another household object whose maximum turn is exactly a quarter turn and justify.

exercise.description: For each object (clothes clip, door with hinge, tongs, scissors, file cover) tick the maximum possible turn: less than 1/4, exactly 1/4, or more than 1/4.

items.prompt: Look at the corner of your notebook. What type of angle does that corner show? How do you know using what you know about turns?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A right angle. The corner of a notebook is a square corner, which is produced by exactly a quarter turn, and a quarter turn gives a right angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A quarter turn produces a right angle; the notebook corner is a square corner, which is exactly a quarter turn.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child fold a piece of paper to make a right angle and compare it to the notebook corner; stretch: find one angle in the classroom that is acute and one that is obtuse and justify each.

exercise.description: Look at angles A–H marked on the notebook-cover house. Write whether each is right, acute, or obtuse.

items.prompt: Kedar opens a fan to a small acute angle and then opens it a little more, still keeping it in the acute range. Can the two acute angles together always stay acute?

options.label: B
options.text: No, two acute angles can together form a right angle or an obtuse angle.

options.label: C
options.text: Two acute angles always add up to a straight angle.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, two acute angles always add up to another acute angle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No, two acute angles can together form a right angle or an obtuse angle. For example, two angles of 1/8 turn each add to 2/8, which is a right angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the fractions of a turn: two 1/8 turns give 2/8, a right angle; two 3/16 turns give 6/16, larger than a right angle.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student assumes combining same-type angles preserves the type, not recognising that the sum can exceed a quarter turn.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student over-generalises and thinks two acute angles always reach the maximum of a straight angle.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student holds a misconception that angle types are fixed and cannot be composed.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child use a fan to show two small acute openings and measure the combined opening; stretch: find which two equal acute turn-fractions add to exactly a right angle.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Do acute-turns question, p.35
exercise.description: Make an acute turn with straws or fan, then make another acute turn. Determine whether the two acute turns together can form another acute turn.

items.prompt: Using an eighths measuring tool, a student places the 1/8 sector on an angle and finds it fits twice with a little space left over. What can she say about the size of the angle? Is it acute, right, or obtuse?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The angle is between 2/8 and 3/8 of a full turn. Since 2/8 is a right angle and 3/8 is more than a right angle, the angle is obtuse.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The angle is greater than 2/8 (right angle) and less than 3/8, placing it in the obtuse range.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child place the 1/8 card on a drawn angle and count the sectors; stretch: ask what measure in eighths would give exactly a right angle and verify.

exercise.description: Guess the measure of each angle shown; then check using the angle-measuring tool (use combinations). State whether each is acute, right, or obtuse.

items.prompt: A triangle has three angles. Two of them measure 1/8 and 2/8 of a full turn. What is the measure of the third angle, in eighths of a full turn? Name its type.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The three angles of a triangle add to a half turn (4/8). So the third angle = 4/8 − 1/8 − 2/8 = 1/8 of a full turn. A 1/8 turn is less than a quarter turn (2/8), so the angle is acute.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The angles of a triangle sum to a half turn (4/8); subtract the two known angles to find the third.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the 4/8 total as a bar and shade off 1/8 and 2/8 to see what remains; stretch: check by placing the three sector tools together to confirm they make a straight (half-turn) angle.

exercise.description: Measure each angle in the given shapes (a), (b), (c). Write measures in terms of turns; describe each as acute, obtuse, or right.

items.section_title: Angle Measuring Tool — Sixths and Twelfths
items.prompt: A circle shows an arrow that has finished a 1/4 turn and is now pointing to the right. Draw or describe where the arrow was pointing before it made the 1/4 turn.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The arrow was pointing upward (North). A quarter turn clockwise from up gives right; so reversing — going a quarter turn anti-clockwise from right — gives up.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reverse the quarter turn: if a 1/4 clockwise turn ends at right, the starting position is one quarter anti-clockwise from right, which is up.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child physically point right and turn back a quarter turn to feel the starting direction; stretch: draw the starting position for a 1/8 turn that ends pointing right.

exercise.description: In circles showing endpoints of 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 turns, draw arrows to show the starting points.

items.prompt: A ladybird faces left. It makes a quarter turn clockwise. Which direction does it face after the turn?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Up. A clockwise quarter turn from left goes to up (the sequence clockwise is right → down → left → up → right…; one step back in that sequence from left gives up).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the clockwise sequence: right, down, left, up; a quarter clockwise turn from left moves to up.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student applies an anti-clockwise quarter turn from left instead of clockwise.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student does not apply any turn, leaving the direction unchanged.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student moves one step in the wrong direction along the clockwise cycle.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child draw the four compass directions in a circle and trace the clockwise path with a finger; stretch: ask what two turns could also bring the ladybird to face up from left.

exercise.description: For each of the four creature pairs making a quarter turn, tick whether the movement is clockwise or anti-clockwise.

items.prompt: Anand starts facing South. He makes one right-angle turn anti-clockwise and then another right-angle turn anti-clockwise. Which direction does he face now?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: North. Anti-clockwise from South goes to East, then another anti-clockwise quarter turn from East goes to North.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the anti-clockwise sequence: South → East → North; two quarter turns anti-clockwise from South land on North.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child stand facing south and make each physical turn; stretch: find the starting direction from which two anti-clockwise right-angle turns land on South.

exercise.description: Complete the table: given starting direction and turns (e.g., 'North, two right angles clockwise'), fill in the ending direction for all 7 rows.

items.prompt: Padma faces North. She makes a half turn clockwise. Which direction does she face? Write one other sequence of turns she could make to end up facing the same direction.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She faces South. One alternative: two quarter turns clockwise from North also give South.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A half turn reverses the facing direction; two quarter turns in the same direction equal a half turn.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child use the wall labels to verify each turn physically; stretch: find a third sequence using anti-clockwise turns that also ends at South from North.

exercise.description: Padma faces the toy shop. Determine what place she faces after a half turn clockwise. Find another way she can turn to face the same place.

items.prompt: Which of the following is the correct angle type for a turn of 1/8 of a full circle?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Acute angle. 1/8 of a full turn is less than 2/8 (the right angle benchmark), so the angle is acute.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare 1/8 to 2/8 (right angle): since 1/8 < 2/8, the angle is acute.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses 1/8 with 2/8, the right-angle fraction.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student applies the straight-angle label to an unfamiliar fraction without comparing to the 4/8 benchmark.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student thinks any turn expressed as a fraction is obtuse, without placing it relative to the right-angle benchmark.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child count fold lines on the eighths tool up to 1 and compare to the right-angle line at 2; stretch: list all eighths-turn fractions that give an acute angle.

exercise.description: Draw angles for given measures of turns (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/12, 1/4) using the given lines.

items.prompt: Draw the angle formed by a turn of 1/2 + 1/4 of a full circle. Label the angle with its fraction of a full turn and name its type.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1/2 + 1/4 = 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4 of a full turn. A 3/4 turn is more than a straight angle (1/2 turn) and less than a full turn. The drawn angle is a reflex-type opening (3/4 of a circle), labelled 3/4. At the preparatory stage this is recognised as more than a straight angle; accept 'more than a straight angle' as a correct description.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the fractions: 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4; draw two rays from a point with 3/4 of a full turn between them.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child use sector tools end-to-end (4/8 + 2/8 = 6/8 = 3/4) to set the angle before drawing; stretch: draw 1/8 + 1/6 and name its type, converting to twelfths to add.

exercise.description: Draw the angles formed by: 1/2, 1/4, 2/4, 1/6, 4/6, 3/12, 1/2+1/4, and 1/8+1/6 turns in your notebook.

items.prompt: The minute hand of a clock makes a full turn in 60 minutes. How many minutes does it take to make a turn of 1/6 of a full circle? Write only the number of minutes.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 10 minutes. 1/6 of 60 minutes = 60 ÷ 6 = 10 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total minutes for a full turn (60) by the denominator of the fraction (6).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a clock face and shade 1/6 of it to count how many 10-minute sections fit; stretch: find how many minutes the hand takes to make a 4/6 turn and check by adding four 10-minute intervals.

exercise.description: Find the turn made by the minute hand for each time interval [(a) 15 min, (b) 30 min, (c) 45 min, (d) 1/12 full turn → ? min, (e) full turn → ? min, (f) 1/6 full turn → ? min, (g) 4/12 full turn → ? min]; draw final clock positions.
